hint: One small step changed it all
funFact: Did you know? Armstrong's bootprints are still up there — the Moon has no wind or rain to wash them away, so they'll last millions of years.

hint: An unsinkable promise, broken by ice
funFact: Did you know? The Titanic's orchestra kept playing as the ship went down. All eight musicians drowned. None were paid for their final shift.

hint: A divided city reunited overnight
funFact: Did you know? East Germans didn't just walk through — they brought hammers. 'Mauerspechte' (wall woodpeckers) chipped souvenirs for months.

hint: A dream spoken to a quarter million
funFact: Did you know? King's most famous line, 'I have a dream', wasn't in the prepared speech. Mahalia Jackson shouted for it and he went off-script.

hint: The longest day on five beaches
funFact: Did you know? Eisenhower carried a pre-written resignation note in case D-Day failed, taking full blame. He never needed to hand it over.

hint: A fortress-prison stormed by revolution
funFact: Did you know? The Bastille held only seven prisoners the day it was stormed, including one convicted of incest and four forgers.

hint: Three ships found a continent by mistake
funFact: Did you know? Columbus never admitted he hadn't reached Asia. To his dying day he insisted the Caribbean was somewhere off the coast of India.

hint: A morning that changed airport security forever
funFact: Did you know? Every US commercial flight was grounded within two hours — around 4,500 planes. Airspace stayed closed for nearly three days.

hint: A motorcade in Dallas ended an era
funFact: Did you know? Jackie Kennedy refused to change out of her blood-stained pink Chanel suit. 'Let them see what they've done,' she said.

hint: A blinding flash over a Japanese city
funFact: Did you know? The Hiroshima bomb's core was a grapefruit-sized lump of uranium. Less than 2% of it actually fissioned.

hint: Westminster Abbey crowned a new era
funFact: Did you know? The Queen's coronation was the first ever televised — a choice she pushed for despite Churchill and Parliament opposing it.

hint: Thirteen colonies signed their freedom
funFact: Did you know? Most signers didn't actually sign on July 4. The famous signing ceremony happened nearly a month later, on August 2, 1776.

hint: A battlefield in Belgium ended an emperor
funFact: Did you know? Napoleon was defeated partly by rain. Wet ground delayed his artillery and gave Prussian reinforcements time to arrive.

hint: 108 minutes orbiting Earth for the first time
funFact: Did you know? Gagarin ejected from his capsule at 7km altitude and parachuted down separately — a fact the Soviets hid for years to claim records.

hint: Fireworks, fear of bugs, and a new millennium
funFact: Did you know? Programmers were so worried about Y2K that over $300 billion was spent worldwide. When midnight struck, almost nothing broke.

hint: A bullet in Sarajevo lit the fuse
funFact: Did you know? The assassin's car had taken a wrong turn. Franz Ferdinand was shot because his driver stopped to reverse — right next to the gunman.

hint: The eleventh hour of the eleventh day
funFact: Did you know? The Armistice was literally signed at 5am but didn't take effect until 11am. Nearly 11,000 soldiers died in those final six hours.

hint: A glass rectangle in your pocket changed everything
funFact: Did you know? Steve Jobs insisted the iPhone have no physical keyboard. Most engineers thought customers would hate it. Over 2 billion sold since.

hint: A Norman duke claimed England's throne
funFact: Did you know? William the Conqueror's coronation ended in chaos — cheering crowds outside were mistaken for a riot, and soldiers set London alight.

hint: Barrels of gunpowder beneath Parliament
funFact: Did you know? Guy Fawkes was the explosives expert, not the mastermind. He was caught at midnight guarding 36 barrels of gunpowder in the cellar.

hint: England's finest 90 minutes — and a few more
event: England wins the FIFA World Cup
funFact: Did you know? England's World Cup win was nearly voided — the winning goal in extra time probably didn't fully cross the line. Debate still rages.

hint: Reactor number four couldn't be contained
funFact: Did you know? The Chernobyl exclusion zone is now one of Europe's largest wildlife sanctuaries. Wolves, lynx, and bison have reclaimed it.

hint: 27 years behind bars, then a walk to freedom
funFact: Did you know? After 27 years in prison, Mandela still had to adjust to tiny things — like an electric toothbrush, which he'd never seen before.

hint: 73 seconds after liftoff, the sky split in two
funFact: Did you know? The Challenger was destroyed by a 25-cent rubber O-ring that froze stiff in unusually cold Florida weather the night before launch.

hint: A meadow by the Thames, a king's hand forced to sign
funFact: Did you know? King John didn't actually sign the Magna Carta — he sealed it with wax. Most people couldn't write, including kings.

hint: A tunnel in Paris and a people's princess
funFact: Did you know? Diana's funeral was watched by over 2.5 billion people live — one of the largest broadcast audiences in human history at the time.

hint: A harbour full of tea, dumped in protest
funFact: Did you know? The Boston Tea Party destroyed 342 chests of tea worth about $1.7 million in today's money. Protestors dressed as Mohawks to disguise themselves.

hint: The final shuttle touched down for good
funFact: Did you know? The Space Shuttle fleet flew 135 missions over 30 years. Atlantis, the last to land, is now on display — still scorched from re-entry.

hint: The rainbow nation inaugurated its first
funFact: Did you know? At his inauguration, Mandela invited his white former jailer to sit in the front row as a VIP guest. The jailer cried.

hint: Dancing in the streets of London and beyond
funFact: Did you know? London threw a massive street party for VE Day, and a young Princess Elizabeth snuck out of the palace to join the celebrating crowds incognito.

hint: A beeping sphere started the space race
funFact: Did you know? Sputnik 1 orbited for only three months, but its radio beep could be heard by ham radio operators worldwide — triggering an American panic.

hint: Tanks crossed a border, igniting a war
funFact: Did you know? Poland's cavalry actually did charge tanks — but only once, and with anti-tank rifles. The 'lances vs. panzers' image is mostly myth.

hint: Wall Street panicked and fortunes vanished
funFact: Did you know? The Wall Street Crash wiped out billions, but many 'suicide jumping from skyscrapers' stories were invented later. Most jumps never happened.

hint: A signature on the USS Missouri ended a global conflict
funFact: Did you know? Japan's surrender was signed on the USS Missouri — which was only 2 years old. The ink pen used is now in the Naval Academy museum.

hint: A new nation was proclaimed in the Middle East
event: Creation of the State of Israel
funFact: Did you know? Israel was declared minutes before the British Mandate expired. The US recognised it 11 minutes later — faster than its own State Department expected.

hint: A proclamation made millions forever free
funFact: Did you know? The Emancipation Proclamation technically only freed slaves in Confederate states, not Union ones. Full abolition took the 13th Amendment in 1865.

hint: Cannons fired on Fort Sumter divided a nation
event: Start of the American Civil War
funFact: Did you know? The first shots of the Civil War caused zero casualties — but a cannon misfire during the surrender ceremony killed one Union soldier.

hint: A shot in a theater shocked the Union
funFact: Did you know? John Wilkes Booth's brother Edwin had actually saved Lincoln's son Robert from a train platform accident months earlier.

hint: A confederation brought provinces together in the north
funFact: Did you know? Canada's flag wasn't designed until 1965 — for nearly a century, it flew the British Red Ensign instead of the maple leaf.

hint: A treaty in a palace ended the Great War
event: Signing of the Treaty of Versailles
funFact: Did you know? The Treaty of Versailles was signed in the Hall of Mirrors — the same room where Germany had proclaimed its empire in 1871. The humiliation was deliberate.

hint: A date which will live in infamy
funFact: Did you know? Pearl Harbor's attack plans were found weeks before by a US intelligence officer — but the memo was filed under 'routine' and never forwarded.

hint: Justice sought in a German city post-war
funFact: Did you know? The Nuremberg trials introduced simultaneous translation — new technology at the time, with interpreters working in sealed glass booths.

hint: A charter signed in San Francisco to unite nations
funFact: Did you know? The UN Charter was signed by 50 nations in San Francisco. Poland signed two months late and is still counted as an original member.

hint: A dreamer was lost on a balcony in Memphis
event: Assassination of Martin Luther King Jr.
funFact: Did you know? MLK's last meal was catfish, and his killer was caught at Heathrow Airport two months later — trying to fly to white-ruled Rhodesia.

hint: Two brothers took flight in Kitty Hawk
funFact: Did you know? The Wright Brothers' first flight lasted just 12 seconds and covered 120 feet — shorter than the wingspan of a modern jumbo jet.

hint: A canal opened, connecting two vast oceans
funFact: Did you know? The Panama Canal cost 25,000 lives to build — mostly from malaria and yellow fever. It also lowered world sea levels by a tiny amount.

hint: A revolutionary car rolled off the assembly line
event: Introduction of the Ford Model T
funFact: Did you know? The Model T came in any colour you wanted, as long as it was black. Black paint dried fastest, so it kept the assembly line moving.

hint: The Spirit of St. Louis crossed the Atlantic solo
funFact: Did you know? Lindbergh's plane had no front windshield — he had to fly 33 hours using a periscope to see forward. He battled sleep by flying inches from the waves.

hint: Three leaders met in Crimea to reshape Europe
funFact: Did you know? At Yalta, Roosevelt was already dying of heart failure. He died just two months later, and critics argue Stalin out-negotiated him ruthlessly.

hint: A mysterious illness was first reported in California
funFact: Did you know? AIDS was initially called 'GRID' — Gay-Related Immune Deficiency — before doctors realised it affected many different groups.

hint: A massive quake and a nuclear crisis in the east
funFact: Did you know? The Fukushima tsunami was taller than some office buildings — up to 14 metres. The plant's sea wall was built to stop waves half that size.

hint: A mountain erupted, burying an ancient city in ash
funFact: Did you know? Vesuvius buried Pompeii under 6 metres of ash, freezing everything in place. Archaeologists still find loaves of bread inside ancient ovens.

hint: Beware the Ides of March, said a seer to an emperor
funFact: Did you know? Caesar was stabbed 23 times, but a Roman doctor later concluded only one wound was fatal — a thrust to the chest by an unknown conspirator.

hint: Ninety-five theses on a door sparked a reformation
funFact: Did you know? Luther probably didn't nail his theses to the door — he more likely mailed them to his archbishop. The hammer story was popularised decades later.

hint: The double helix structure of life was unveiled
funFact: Did you know? Rosalind Franklin's X-ray photo was shown to Watson and Crick without her permission. She didn't share the Nobel — she'd died of cancer at 37.

hint: A graphical operating system changed personal computing
funFact: Did you know? Windows 1.0 shipped two years late and was mocked as a 'bad joke' — it didn't even properly overlap windows. Version 3.0 finally made it take off.

hint: The earth shook and flames consumed the golden city
funFact: Did you know? San Francisco's earthquake tilted gas lines and started fires that raged for three days. Most damage came from the fires, not the shaking.

hint: Footprints left in the lunar dust for the very first time
funFact: Did you know? Buzz Aldrin's first act on the Moon was communion. He poured wine and ate bread he'd brought from his church — privately, off mic.

hint: Terror struck the Olympic Games in Munich
funFact: Did you know? The Munich attackers had trained in Libya. The German rescue operation used only five snipers for eight terrorists — all hostages died.

hint: A landmark decision on reproductive rights in the US
funFact: Did you know? Roe v. Wade was decided 7–2. The 'Jane Roe' plaintiff, Norma McCorvey, later reversed her views and campaigned to overturn her own case.

hint: A president resigned to avoid certain impeachment
funFact: Did you know? Nixon resigned at 9:01am — the first US president ever to do so. He left the White House by helicopter and never publicly apologised.

hint: Helicopters evacuated an embassy ending a long war
funFact: Did you know? The famous 'helicopter on a roof' photo from Saigon wasn't the US Embassy — it was a CIA safe house two blocks away.

hint: Hostages taken in a volatile embassy shift
funFact: Did you know? The Iran hostage crisis lasted exactly 444 days. The hostages were released minutes after Reagan's inauguration, snubbing Carter one last time.

hint: A telescope launched to gaze into deep space
funFact: Did you know? Hubble was launched with a tiny flaw in its mirror — 1/50th the thickness of a human hair. A shuttle mission flew up in 1993 to fit it with glasses.

hint: Forces invaded a neighbor, starting a desert storm
funFact: Did you know? Iraq invaded Kuwait partly over a straw — accusing Kuwait of slant-drilling to steal Iraqi oil across the border. The invasion lasted two days.

hint: A truck bomb echoed through twin towers
funFact: Did you know? The 1993 WTC bombing killed six people and injured over 1,000 — but the towers didn't fall. Engineers cited the explosion's ground-floor placement.

hint: A domestic terror attack shattered an Oklahoma city
funFact: Did you know? Timothy McVeigh's truck bomb was made from fertiliser, diesel, and a rental truck. It killed 168 people, including 19 children in a daycare.

hint: A sheep was born, cloned from an adult cell
funFact: Did you know? Dolly the sheep was named after Dolly Parton — because she was cloned from a mammary gland cell. Scientists thought it was hilarious.

hint: A new currency was adopted across twelve nations
funFact: Did you know? Euro banknotes don't depict real bridges — the designs show generic architectural styles, since no single real bridge could represent all of Europe.

hint: A coalition launched a strike to topple a regime
funFact: Did you know? The 2003 Iraq invasion was launched with 'shock and awe' bombing, but Baghdad fell to ground troops just 21 days after it began.

hint: A massive wave devastated shores across the ocean
funFact: Did you know? The 2004 Boxing Day tsunami travelled at 800 km/h underwater — jet speed — and raised the day's length by 2.68 microseconds by redistributing Earth's mass.

hint: Hope and change elected the first black president
funFact: Did you know? Obama's 2008 campaign raised over $750 million — more than the previous two elections combined — mostly in small online donations.

hint: An iconic cathedral burned but did not shatter
funFact: Did you know? Notre-Dame's main spire collapsed but its three famous rose windows survived. Beekeepers on the roof discovered their bees had also survived the flames.

hint: A viral outbreak was declared global by the WHO
funFact: Did you know? The word 'pandemic' comes from Greek 'pan-demos' meaning 'all the people'. COVID was the first WHO-declared pandemic since 2009.

hint: A nation woke to an invasion on its eastern flank
funFact: Did you know? Russia called its invasion a 'special military operation'. Using the word 'war' in Russian media became punishable by up to 15 years in prison.

hint: An independent city-state was born in Rome
funFact: Did you know? Vatican City is smaller than a typical 9-hole golf course — 0.49 sq km — and has its own post office, train station, and ATM with Latin menus.

hint: A flight claimed to be first over the northern pole
funFact: Did you know? Byrd's claim to have flown over the North Pole is now widely disputed — his own flight log had suspicious erasures. He may have turned back early.

hint: A Norwegian team reached the southernmost point
funFact: Did you know? Amundsen's team reached the South Pole using sled dogs, which they also ate along the way — planning the calories into the expedition from the start.

hint: The highest peak on Earth was finally conquered
funFact: Did you know? Hillary and Tenzing never publicly revealed who stepped on Everest's summit first. They agreed to always say they did it 'together'.

hint: A grey box from IBM redefined personal computing
funFact: Did you know? The original IBM PC shipped with only 16 KB of RAM — about 0.000002% of a modern laptop. It cost $1,565, or $5,000 in today's money.

hint: An exiled emperor passed away on a remote island
funFact: Did you know? Napoleon died on Saint Helena at 51, likely from stomach cancer. His hair tested positive for arsenic, but probably from wallpaper dye, not poison.

hint: Two great minds: one of evolution, one of emancipation, born today
funFact: Did you know? Charles Darwin and Abraham Lincoln were born the exact same day — 12 February 1809 — and both reshaped how humanity saw itself.

hint: An ultimate surrender at a courthouse ended the war
funFact: Did you know? At Appomattox, Grant let Lee's soldiers keep their horses so they could go home and plant crops. It's still cited as a model of post-war grace.

hint: A golden spike united the east and west coasts
funFact: Did you know? The 'golden spike' was actually not solid gold — just plated. And it was pulled back out of the rail minutes after the ceremony photo was taken.

hint: The final major clash of the American Indian Wars
funFact: Did you know? Wounded Knee ended with the US Army awarding 20 Medals of Honor. Native American groups still campaign to have them revoked to this day.

hint: A Hawaiian queen was overthrown by a committee
funFact: Did you know? Queen Liliuokalani spent years under house arrest in her own palace after the coup — and filled the time composing songs, including 'Aloha Oe'.

hint: A sunken battleship ignited a war with Spain
funFact: Did you know? The USS Maine probably exploded from an internal coal fire, not a Spanish mine — but 'Remember the Maine!' worked great as a war slogan anyway.

hint: A devastating hurricane swept through a Texas island
funFact: Did you know? The Galveston Hurricane killed over 6,000 people — still the deadliest natural disaster in US history. The city rebuilt by raising itself 17 feet higher.

hint: America officially joined the immense Great War
funFact: Did you know? By the time America joined WWI, Europe had already been fighting for nearly three years. US troops called themselves 'Doughboys'.

hint: A treaty took Russia out of a global conflict
funFact: Did you know? Brest-Litovsk cost Russia a third of its population and most of its industry — but Lenin signed anyway, betting Germany would lose the war. He won the bet.

hint: A period began where certain spirits ran dry by law
event: Start of Prohibition in the US
funFact: Did you know? Prohibition boosted organised crime spectacularly. Al Capone's bootlegging operation earned him an estimated $100 million a year — tax-free.

hint: The 19th amendment guaranteed a woman's right to vote
funFact: Did you know? The 19th Amendment passed by one vote in Tennessee — and that vote came from a legislator whose mother had sent him a letter begging him to support it.

hint: An unsealed tomb revealed a boy king's golden mask
funFact: Did you know? Howard Carter first peered into Tut's tomb by candlelight. When asked what he saw, he replied: 'Yes, wonderful things.'

hint: A groundbreaking friendly computer was introduced
funFact: Did you know? The Mac's famous '1984' Super Bowl ad only aired once nationally. Apple's board hated it — Steve Jobs ran it anyway.

hint: A treaty united nations under a new European banner
funFact: Did you know? Maastricht created the European Union and paved the way for the euro. The UK and Denmark negotiated opt-outs — the UK later used its opt-out to leave entirely.

hint: A free encyclopedia emerged to organize knowledge
funFact: Did you know? Wikipedia's first edit was the word 'Hello, World!' — and the site was originally meant as a side project to feed articles into a more formal encyclopedia called Nupedia.

hint: A social network was born in a dorm room
funFact: Did you know? Facebook started as 'Thefacebook' and was restricted to Harvard students for weeks. The 'the' was dropped after the company paid $200,000 for facebook.com.

hint: The first video broadcast shared a trip to the zoo
funFact: Did you know? The first YouTube video is called 'Me at the zoo' — 19 seconds of co-founder Jawed Karim talking about elephants. It still gets millions of views.

hint: A probe provided our first close look at a distant dwarf
funFact: Did you know? New Horizons took 9 years to reach Pluto, travelling at 58,000 km/h. Its flyby lasted just a few hours, but it gathered 16 months of data to send home.

hint: Tragedy struck an arena in Manchester post-concert
funFact: Did you know? The Manchester Arena bomb went off as fans left an Ariana Grande concert. Grande returned two weeks later for a benefit concert watched by 50 million.
